1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6.name: English Defence
1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6.background: The Leicester player P. N. Wallis investigated the opening in the late 1940s and early 1950s, and in the 1970s it was taken up by leading English players such as Tony Miles and Raymond Keene. Viktor Korchnoi used it successfully in game 6 of his Candidates semi-final match against Lev Polugaevsky at Évian in 1977.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6 3.e4.strategy: Takes the broad pawn centre at once, which is exactly what the English Defence invites. Black plans to undermine it from a distance, starting with the bishop on b7 hitting e4, so White gains space but has to keep the centre pawns protected.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6 3.Nc3.strategy: Develops a piece and controls e4, so Black's fianchettoed bishop meets resistance on the long diagonal. White gives up the immediate broad pawn centre for a flexible set-up in which Black can pin the knight and the fight turns on who controls e4.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6 3.Nc3 Bb7.strategy: Puts the bishop on the long diagonal at once, where it eyes e4 and the whole centre from a distance. Black lets White build a pawn centre and prepares to attack it, and keeps the pin of the knight in reserve.

1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6 3.Nc3 d5.strategy: Takes the centre directly with a classical, solid set-up. But the pawn on d5 is pressed at once by White's c-pawn and knight, and it blocks the diagonal the b6 plan wants for the bishop. Sound, if less ambitious than undermining the centre from afar.
1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6 3.Nc3 d5.name: Queen's Gambit Declined: Alapin Variation

1.d4 e6 2.c4 b6 3.e4 Bb7.strategy: The point of the opening: the bishop attacks the e4 pawn at once, and nothing defends it yet. White must spend a move on the pawn, while Black has developed a piece and set up a long-term target.
